passages.happening:
‘Many years later, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra son of Seraiah’ (verse 1) appears, and his family line is traced back through the priests to ‘the son of Aaron the chief priest’ (verse 5).

‘This Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given. The king had granted Ezra all his requests, for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him’ (verse 6).

In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, Ezra goes up to Jerusalem with a company of Israelites, among them priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants (verse 7). He sets out from Babylon on the first day of the first month, and he arrives in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, ‘for the gracious hand of his God was upon him’ (verse 9).

Then the verse that tells who he is: ‘For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 6 ended with the temple finished in 515 BC. Chapter 7 opens ‘Many years later’ (verse 1), and the gap is about fifty-seven years, the years in which the story of Esther takes place elsewhere in the empire. The first half of the book was about rebuilding the house of God. The second half is about rebuilding the people around the law of God, and only now, more than halfway through, does the man the book is named for appear.

His family line runs back to Aaron, but it is shortened. It skips several generations known from 1 Chronicles 6, as ancient family lists often did. His father is named as Seraiah, the chief priest the Babylonians executed in 587 or 586 BC. That was more than a century before Ezra's arrival, so son here means descendant.

A scribe in the ancient world was more than a copyist. Scribes were trained in writing, law and administration, and they served temples and royal courts. In Ezra the word gains a new sense: a scribe of the law of Moses, a scholar of Scripture whose skill lies in understanding and teaching it. The scribes who appear in the Gospels, the experts in the law, look back to him.

The road from Babylon to Jerusalem followed the Euphrates northwest and then turned south: roughly 900 miles, and four months on the way.

And notice the refrain that begins here, the hand of the LORD upon him (verses 6 and 9). The book uses it for God's active guidance through ordinary things: a king's goodwill, a safe road, the courage to gather others. In verse 10 the order matters. Study leads to practice, and practice to teaching. The verb for study, darash, means to seek, and later Jewish tradition took its word midrash, the interpretation of Scripture, from it. For Ezra, study was a way of seeking God.
passages.later: When Ezra later read the law to the whole people in Jerusalem, the Levites helped them understand it: ‘So they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read’ (Nehemiah 8:8).
passages.hard:
When did Ezra come to Jerusalem?

The book says that Ezra came ‘in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes’ (verse 7). The traditional view, still the most widely held, takes the king as Artaxerxes I, who reigned from 465 to 424 BC. His seventh year was 458 BC, so Ezra came thirteen years before Nehemiah. Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, which would date Ezra to 398 BC, after Nehemiah. A few propose that the text once read the thirty-seventh year of Artaxerxes I, about 428 BC.

The debate turns on how Ezra and Nehemiah relate in Nehemiah 8 and 12, where they appear together, and on the names of the high priests in the period. Careful readers hold each view, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: Study, practice, teach: in that order. Ask which of the three comes most easily to you, and which you are tempted to skip. And ask what it would mean to set your heart, as Ezra did, on understanding God's word and living it before telling others what it says.

passages.happening:
The chapter quotes the letter King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra. It opens, ‘Artaxerxes, king of kings. To Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven: Greetings’ (verse 12).

Any Israelites who wish to go, priests and Levites among them, may go with Ezra to Jerusalem (verse 13). He is sent by the king and his seven counselors ‘to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand’ (verse 14). He is to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, ‘whose dwelling is in Jerusalem’ (verse 15), with gifts from the province of Babylon and the freewill offerings of the people and priests. With it he is to buy animals for the sacrifices, and anything else the house of God needs may be paid for from the royal treasury (verses 17-20).

The king orders his treasurers west of the Euphrates to supply what Ezra asks, within set limits, ‘and salt without limit’ (verse 22). ‘Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven must be done diligently for His house. For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons?’ (verse 23). And no tax may be laid on the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, temple servants or other servants of the house of God (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The letter is written in Aramaic, the language of the empire's business, and it fits what is known of Persian practice. Persian kings supported local temples and sometimes gave local laws the backing of the crown. An Egyptian official named Udjahorresnet recorded on his statue, now in the Vatican Museums, that Darius I had sent him back to Egypt to restore a place of learning at Sais. It is a close parallel: a Persian king sending a learned subject home with royal support.

The seven counselors recall the seven nobles of Persia and Media in the book of Esther. Whether Ezra's title of scribe was also an official Persian post, as some scholars have suggested, is debated.

The king's reason is plain in verse 23. In the ancient world, honoring a people's god was thought to protect the empire. Artaxerxes does not want the God of heaven angry with his realm.
passages.later:
The book of Esther names the same kind of royal council: ‘the seven princes of Persia and Media who had personal access to the king and ranked highest in the kingdom’ (Esther 1:14).

And the same king later sent Nehemiah with letters too: ‘If it pleases the king, may letters be given to me for the governors west of the Euphrates’ (Nehemiah 2:7).
passages.asks: A foreign king paid for worship he did not share, partly from goodwill and partly from fear. Ask how you receive help from people whose reasons are not your own. And ask what it would mean to give to the worship of God as freely as this king gave.

passages.happening:
The letter ends with Ezra's commission. ‘And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God which you possess, are to appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates’ (verse 25). ‘And you are to teach these laws to anyone who does not know them’ (verse 25).

Anyone who does not keep ‘the law of your God and the law of the king’ (verse 26) is to face strict judgment, from imprisonment to death.

Then Ezra speaks for himself. ‘Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem’ (verse 27). God has shown him favor before the king and his officials. ‘And because the hand of the LORD my God was upon me, I took courage and gathered the leaders of Israel to return with me’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
At verse 27 the book returns from Aramaic to Hebrew, and the voice changes. From here to the end of chapter 9, Ezra tells his own story in the first person. Scholars call these chapters the Ezra Memoir.

The king's letter uses a Persian word, dat, for law. In verse 26 the law of God and the law of the king stand side by side. The Persian empire gave legal force to the religious laws of its peoples, and Ezra's commission fits that practice. In the book of Esther the same word is used for the laws of the Medes and Persians.

Ezra's first words in the book are praise to God, not a tribute to the king. It was the LORD who put it into the king's heart. And the favor of God turns into courage. Ezra gathers leaders because the hand of the LORD was upon him.
passages.later: The book of Esther uses the same word for the laws of the Medes and Persians, which could not be repealed: ‘let it be recorded in the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be repealed’ (Esther 1:19).
passages.hard:
A foreign king gives Ezra power to enforce God's law, with penalties up to death. What should a reader make of that?

This is a Persian king's decree for a province of his empire, and the book records it as the empire's grant of authority. Persia gave legal force to the religious laws of its peoples, and Ezra's commission fits that practice. The book's own weight falls elsewhere: on teaching the law to those who do not know it (verse 25), and on Ezra's thanks to God (verse 27).

The decree is not a pattern for any government or church today. Nothing here gives anyone a warrant to force faith on others by threat or harm.
passages.asks: Ezra thanked God for a king's favor, and then he took courage. Ask whether you thank God for the help that comes to you through other people. And ask what courage that help has given you, and what you have done with it.
